content:

A Samsung LPDDR5X memory chip - Image Credit: Samsung

title: Apple posts record revenue on strong iPhone, Mac sales
content:
Macworld





After a jam-packed month that included the launch of a new smart-home display, touch-screen laptop, and folding phone, Apple on Monday released impressive quarterly results leading into what should be a stellar holiday quarter. For the quarter ending September 30, which notably doesn’t include any of the above products, Apple posted revenue of  $114.5 billion, a 12 percent increase over the same quarter last year and a massive close to its “best fiscal year ever,” according to CEO John Ternus. 
Leading the way, as expected, was iPhone sales. With the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro boosting the numbers, Apple posted 57.5 billion in revenue compared to 49 billion last year, a 17 percent increase. The quarter includes roughly two weeks of iPhone 18 Pro preorders and sales, but doesn’t include any iPhone Duo orders, which didn’t go on sale until October 16.
Also hitting shelves this quarter was the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, but those didn’t have nearly as big of an impact. Sales in the Wearable, Home, and Accessories category were down about 8 percent year-over-year despite the new products. Also down was iPad revenue, which posted an 11 percent decline. The new OLED iPad mini could help stabilize things in the fourth quarter, but the rest of the iPad lineup isn’t expected to get an update until 2027.
The opposite is true for the Mac. Buoyed by the launch of the M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio, Apple posted a strong 25 percent increase year-over-year with earnings of $10.8 billion. Ternus said that Apple has, “never sold more Macs in a fiscal year.” 
That bodes well for the holiday quarter, when the new M6 iMac and MacBook Pro, as well as the new PROLED XDR MacBook arrive. Apple expects revenue to grow 7-10 percent despite “constrained supply,” which would be the best quarter for revenue in the company’s history.
Finally, Apple’s Services category continues to grow. For the first time, Apple topped $30 billion in revenue for Services on growth of around 10 percent.
Apple is holding a conference call at 5 pm ET to discuss the results and the road ahead for its fiscal 2027, so stay tuned for updates.

title: Apple Reports 4Q 2026 Results: $30.7B Profit on $114.5B Revenue
content:
Apple today announced financial results for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026, which corresponds to the third calendar quarter of the year. The quarter included a number of August and September product releases from Apple, as well as the CEO transition from Tim Cook to John Ternus that took place on September 1.


For the quarter, Apple posted revenue of $114.5 billion and net quarterly profit of $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per diluted share, compared to revenue of $102.5 billion and net quarterly profit of $27.5 billion, or $1.85 per diluted share, in the year-ago quarter.

Gross margin for the most recent quarter was 47.9 percent, compared to 47.2 percent in the year-ago quarter. Apple also declared a quarterly dividend payment of $0.27 per share, payable on November 16 to shareholders of record as of November 12.

Apple set September quarter records for total revenue, iPhone revenue, and earnings per share, and an all-time record for Services revenue.

"Today, Apple is proud to report a September quarter revenue record of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago, with iPhone reaching a September quarter record and Services reaching an all-time high, capping off our best fiscal year ever," said John Ternus, Apple's CEO. "We're closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet. That includes the iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original, alongside iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, our most powerful iPhones yet. We also just introduced a whole new generation of hardware for the home and brought Touch to Mac for the first time. Together with the all-new Siri AI, it's an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season."

title: High-end robotic ‘HomeView Ultra’ could land in 2028 for $1,000
content:
Macworld





While we all wait for Apple’s HomeView smart home hub to ship, we’re reminded that Apple has been working on a larger, robotic version of the same thing for years. A new report from The Information shares some details about the so-called “HomeView Ultra” (which has reportedly been floated but may or may not launch under that name).
According to the report, this larger HomeView would have a roughly 9-inch display, giving it about 65 percent more screen area than the 7-inch display on the HomeView. It would be attached to its base via a robotic arm that somewhat resembles the iMac G4 or the Pixar lamp. It would feature cameras and sensors that make it aware of its environment, so it can do things like follow you around during a FaceTime call, turn on lights when someone enters a room, or even shoo the cat off the table.
Apple published a research paper last year showing an R&D project for a robotic lamp with personality, and it’s enough to make you instantly want one. If the robotic HomeView similarly animates and moves as though it has a soul, it might even justify the estimated $1,000 price tag.
The report claims that the device, code-named J595, will ship later next year at the earliest, or perhaps in 2028. Most telling is that the hardware has apparently been more or less complete for two years, but is waiting on the software to catch up. Also, there has apparently been some debate about which features should be in the 1st-generation device and which should wait for the 2nd-gen model. According to The Information, the autonomous AI features are ambitious and not ready yet, so the release timing is all about balancing the AI development with the first-generation feature set.

title: Don’t worry, full-sized iPad fans, the model you want is geting an update soon
content:
Macworld





The announcement of the 8th-gen iPad mini last week included several major improvements on the previous model: a thinner and lighter design, a larger and brighter screen, dust and water resistance, and a big processor upgrade. As is often the case with Apple’s disjointed and confusing iPad range, however, this isolated update leaves the rest of the company’s tablets looking rather out of date.
As the lineup currrenty stands, the baseline iPad has an A16, a full four chip generations behind the mini’s A20 Pro. It can’t run Apple Intelligence or Siri AI and looks thoroughly underpowered. The current iPad Air, meanwhile, costs $50 more than the mini but misses out on the latter’s OLED screen (and nano-texture finish), fast-charge capabilities, and new Acoustic Display feature… plus it’s nowhere near as slim. And the iPad Pro still has an M5 despite the M6 arriving for the MacBook and Mac mini.
But there’s good news for prospective iPad customers, because those older models are reportedly headed towards their own refresh early next year. In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman predicts that Apple “will turn its attention to a slew of other tablet updates in 2027,” going on to specify that these updates will likely happen in the first half of the year.
This means imminent new versions of all three non-mini iPad lines. Gurman offers little detail about the next edition of the baseline iPad, other than to note that recent price hikes have put it well above previously comparable rivals. To justify the pricing, one would imagine a significant boost to the device’s processing muscle is required, which would align with the most recent rumors. 
Gurman is more illuminating on the subject of the next iPad Air, which he expects to switch to OLED in order to match the iPad mini. That would presumably come with a $100 price hike as well, which would put some space between it and the iPad mini.
The most compelling update, perhaps inevitably, will be the “faster” next generation of iPad Pro at the top of the range. “The big change on the high-end machine is likely to be the addition of a vapor chamber to cool things down during gaming and intensive AI tasks,” Gurman writes. The vapor chamber was one of the headline updates in the iPhone 17 Pro last year. The idea that it will make the move to the iPad Pro is a rumor, we should add, that’s been making the rounds since at least 2025.
It isn’t clear how Apple plans to unveil the new iPads. The company has been known to hold a press event in the spring, with the last such event being held in May 2024 to announce the M4 iPad Pro. A reveal at WWDC 2027, which will take place in June, would technically count as the first half of the year, but WWDC usually focuses on software with minimal hardware discussion. Based on the events of last month, however, it may be more likely for Apple to announce the new models via smaller “experiences,” press releases, and quiet updates to its website.
creator: Macworld

title: Best MacBook for 2026: Air vs Pro vs Neo compared
content:
Macworld





Apple sells several MacBook models across different sizes, prices, and performance levels, so choosing the right one depends on your budget, the type of work you do, and how much power you actually need.
In this in-depth guide, we explain which MacBook is best for different users, compare the latest MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and the MacBook Pro models (with and without touchscreen), and help you decide how much RAM and how much storage you really need.
Choosing a MacBook Pro now involves two decisions: how much processing power you need, and which display you want. The entry-level 14-inch model uses the M6 chip, while more demanding users can choose M5 Pro or M5 Max configurations with either a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display or a PROLED XDR OLED touchscreen.
For most people, the MacBook Air remains our recommended starting point. If you need a Pro, choose the chip, memory and storage around your workload, then consider whether the touchscreen model’s OLED display and lighter design justify the extra cost. In this article, we’ll help you decide whether a MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, or MacBook Neo is the best fit for your needs.


Which MacBook is right for you?
In 2026, Apple’s laptop lineup spans five main choices: the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, the mainstream MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro, the high-performance M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro and the touchscreen versions of those MacBook Pro models.
Best for basic use and tight budgets: MacBook Neo is ideal for students, casual browsing, streaming, and light productivity at the lowest entry price.
Best for most people: MacBook Air (M5)  offers the best mix of portability, battery life, silent operation, and everyday performance.
Best for those who want a superior display and extra ports: The MacBook Pro (M6) offers professional-grade features without the extreme power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. 
Best for professionals and power users: MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max) is best for demanding workflows such as 4K video editing, 3D work, heavy multitasking, and software development.
Best for high-end creative professionals: Suited to those who work extensively on their laptop’s built-in display and need direct touch interaction. 
Use the table below to quickly find the MacBook that best suit your needs, or read on for more detailed guide to help you choose the best MacBook for your specific needs.

The MacBook Air (M5) is the best MacBook for most buyers because it offers the strongest balance of price, portability, battery life, and performance.
The 13-inch MacBook Air is light, quiet, fast enough for everyday work, and easier to recommend than any other Mac laptop. The latest version, updated in March 2026, keeps the same winning formula while improving storage and connectivity. There is also a 15-inch version for anyone who wants a larger screen. 
What’s new
The latest MacBook Air features the M5 chip, base storage is 512GB, and it supports newer wireless standards including Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Why we recommend the MacBook Air
Excellent balance of performance and portability
Silent fanless design
Long battery life
Strong everyday performance for work, school, and travel
Now ships with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage as standard
Sizes
The MacBook Air comes in two sizes:
13-inch MacBook Air, 13.6-inch screen: Best for portability
15-inch MacBook Air, 15.3-inch screen: Better for multitasking and split-screen work
Display
As you can see from the above measurements, the display, when measured diagonally is a little larger than the standard naming would suggest. As a result the 13-inch MacBook Air display is actually larger than that on the 13-inch MacBook Neo, discussed below. The MacBook Air uses a bright Liquid Retina display, but it still lacks the 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate and HDR capabilities found on MacBook Pro models.
Performance
The M5 chip in the MacBook Air is fast enough for office work, school tasks, web apps, multitasking, and light creative work. Because the Air has no fan, though, performance can dip during long video exports or other sustained heavy workloads so that the temperature remains optimal.
Battery life
Battery life is excellent, making the Air a great choice for anyone who works away from a desk. It offers more battery life than the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, but falls short of the 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Other specs
You get MagSafe 3 for charging and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The MacBook Air also supports up to two external displays. (Older M1 and M2 models were limited to one external monitor). 
16GB RAM to 32GB RAM
From 512GB to 4TB SSD
Price
Apple put MacBook Air prices up by $200 in June 2026. 
13-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,299/£1,299
15-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,499/£1,499
What to know before buying
The Air’s biggest limitation is sustained performance. It is quick for most tasks, but it is not the right machine for users who regularly push their system for long periods. The MacBook Air is likely to soon adopt the M6 chip as used in the entry-level MacBook Pro, Mac mini and iMac.

The MacBook Neo is the cheapest way to buy a Mac laptop in 2026. Now starting at $699 (which is unfortunately $100 more than it was when Apple launched it in March), it is aimed at students, first-time Mac buyers, and casual users who mainly browse the web, stream video, join video calls, and work in basic apps.
Despite its lower price, it still looks and feels like a MacBook, with an all-aluminum design and a lightweight chassis.
Who is MacBook Neo for?
The MacBook Neo is best for people whose computing needs are simple: web browsing, email, documents, streaming, and schoolwork.
Why we recommend MacBook Neo
Lowest price in the lineup
Light and portable
Quiet fanless design
Good battery life
Fast enough for basic everyday use
Sizes
The MacBook Neo comes in just one size:
13-inch MacBook Neo, 13-inch screen
Display 
Like the MacBook Air the MacBook Neo offers a Liquid Retina display with max 500 nits brightness, but that’s where the similarities end. The display is slightly smaller than the display on the 13-inch MacBook Air, offering 2,408 by 1,506 pixels compared to 2,560 by 1,664 pixels. It also lacks the wide color P3 and True Tone technology of the other MacBooks, offering only sRGB color. 
Performance 
The MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip – the same processor first introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro. While it is a mobile-class chip, its performance is optimized for a laptop environment, offering a highly responsive experience for everyday productivity. In our tests it proved faster than the M3 in single-core, while equal to the M1 when it came to multi-core performance and graphics. 
Battery life 
The MacBook Neo should comfortably last a working day of general productivity. In our video-loop battery test, with screen brightness set to 150 nits, it lasted 13 hours and 15 minutes. Apple advertises up to 16 hours of video streaming or 11 hours of wireless web browsing. More demanding tasks will drain the battery faster.
Other specs
You get two USB-C ports, but these are not identical in capability, one being USB 3 and the other USB 2. See MacBook Neo ports explained. The MacBook Neo only supports one external display with a resolution of up to 4K at 60Hz.

What to know before buying
The Neo makes several trade-offs to achieve its low price, including the absence of a backlit keyboard, a limited selection of ports, and no Touch ID on the base model. It also features a lower-quality display compared to the Air and Pro, offers less memory with a maximum of 8GB RAM, and delivers lower sustained performance than M-series MacBooks. For many buyers, the 512GB, $799 model represents better value, as it includes Touch ID and additional storage.
Alternatives
The MacBook Neo is the best budget MacBook, but it is best suited to light workloads. If you can spend more, the MacBook Air remains the better long-term buy for most people.
Another option, if a low price is your top priority, is a refurbished MacBook. Look out for clearance deals on older Apple silicon MacBooks, but avoid the older Intel-based models. See: MacBook Pro deals and MacBook Air deals.

MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			
The M5 MacBook Air and M6 MacBook Pro are different in some significant ways.

Foundry




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work and light creative projects in a thin, light, silent design. Choose the MacBook Pro if you regularly run demanding workloads or will benefit from its better display and additional ports.
The closest comparison is between the M5 MacBook Air and 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. For more demanding professional work, the MacBook Pro also offers M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with a choice of non-touchscreen or PROLED XDR touchscreen displays.
Performance: Do you need a MacBook Pro?
The M5 MacBook Air is well suited to web browsing, office apps, studying, photo editing, and occasional video projects. Using creative software doesn’t automatically mean you need a Pro: the size of your projects and how frequently you run demanding tasks matter more.
The M6 MacBook Pro combines a newer chip generation with active cooling. Its fans help it sustain performance during lengthy video exports, code compilation, and other intensive tasks. The Air’s fanless design keeps it completely silent, but performance can fall during prolonged heavy workloads.
If these demanding tasks make up much of your working day, consider an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. These offer greater processing, graphics, and memory capacity than the standard M6 model. A newer chip generation doesn’t automatically make the M6 the more powerful choice.
Display and ports: What does the Pro add?
The MacBook Air’s Liquid Retina display is suitable for everyday work, with 500 nits brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate. You can choose a 13-inch model for portability or a 15-inch model for more workspace.
The M6 MacBook Pro’s 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display adds mini-LED technology, deeper contrast, brighter HDR highlights, and ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. These features are particularly useful for viewing and editing HDR content, although you don’t need to be a creative professional to appreciate the screen.
The M6 Pro also provides three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot. The Air has two Thunderbolt 4 ports, so connecting memory cards, HDMI displays, or several accessories may require adapters or a dock.
For an OLED touchscreen, choose a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Touchscreen availability is a separate consideration from how much processing power you need.
Portability, battery life, and price
The Air is thinner and lighter, making it the stronger choice if you carry your laptop regularly. The 15-inch Air is also worth considering if you want a larger screen without the weight and expense of a 16-inch Pro.
The M6 MacBook Pro has a higher advertised battery-life rating, although actual endurance depends on your workload. Both models are suitable for working away from a power socket.
The Air costs less, but compare configurations with matching memory and storage before deciding. The M6 Pro starts with more storage, which narrows the price difference if you would otherwise upgrade the Air.
Our buying advice: Air or Pro?
Buy the MacBook Air for everyday work, studying, travel, and light creative projects. It offers the best balance of performance, portability, and price for most buyers.
Buy the M6 MacBook Pro if you want its HDR display, additional ports, longer advertised battery life, or better sustained performance.
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro for demanding professional workloads that justify more processing power, graphics performance, or memory. Consider the PROLED XDR version if you also want OLED and touch.

Is MacBook Air good enough?

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




The MacBook Air may suffice in some cases: 
Creatives: The Air works well for light creative work, especially photo editing, design, and shorter video projects. It is not as strong in sustained workloads, but it is much easier to carry and costs less.
Development: The MacBook Air is still a good choice for lighter software development, especially for web development, scripting, and general programming. It is best for developers who prioritize portability over maximum sustained speed.
Gaming: The M5 MacBook Air features a third-generation ray-tracing engine and enhanced shader cores, which Apple says improves 3D rendering and gaming tasks. However, in our tests the lack of active cooling caused performance to dip after playing for 10 minutes or so. You can play casual games just fine, but for a variety of reasons, if you’re into AAA gaming, the Air isn’t the best choice.
What about MacBook Neo?
If your budget is much tighter and your needs are basic, the MacBook Neo is the entry point. It gives you macOS at a much lower price, but with more compromises than the Air. If you choose the Neo we recommend the 512GB version.

Other MacBook buying decisions to consider
When buying a MacBook, it’s important to consider how you will use it, as this will determine the right balance of performance, portability, and price. 
Key factors to consider include which chip you require, how much RAM you will need for multitasking, and the size of the SSD required for storage, all of which cannot be upgraded later. 
Screen size affects portability and productivity, screen quality is key for creative work, while battery life matters if you work on the go. You should also think about weight, port selection, and long-term value to ensure the device meets your needs both now and in the future.
In the next section we’ll examine these elements of the buying decision. 


						

							


Best MacBook display and screen size

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The best MacBook screen size depends on how much portability, screen space, and display quality you need.
Best MacBook screen sizes
Best size for most people: 13-inch MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro
Best size for portability: 13-inch MacBook Air or MacBook Neo 
Best all-around Pro size: 14-inch MacBook Pro 
Best large-screen option without Pro pricing: 15-inch MacBook Air 
Best for maximum workspace: 16-inch MacBook Pro 
How many screens are supported 
The 13-inch and 14-inch MacBooks offer the best balance of portability and usability. The larger 15-inch and 16-inch options are ideal if you want more room for spreadsheets, side-by-side apps, or general multitasking. These displays can run alongside the built-in screen. The M5 Pro and M5 Max limits apply to both touchscreen and non-touchscreen models.
MacBook Neo: Supports only one external display up to 4K at 60Hz.
MacBook Air (M5): Supports up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz.
MacBook Pro (M6): Supports up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz.
MacBook Pro (M5 Pro): Supports up to three external displays, each at 6K/60Hz.
MacBook Pro (M5 Max): Supports up to four external displays, each at 6K/60Hz.
For more advice read: How to use two or more monitors to a Mac.
MacBook displays: Liquid Retina, Liquid Retina XDR and PROLED XDR
Apple’s MacBooks offer three main display types. The most useful differences are brightness, contrast, refresh rate and touchscreen support.
Liquid Retina: MacBook Neo and MacBook Air
These displays suit everyday work, web browsing and watching videos. They have a fixed 60Hz refresh rate and don’t support touch. The Air’s display also supports the wider P3 color gamut, making it a better choice than the Neo for color-sensitive work.
Liquid Retina XDR: Non-touchscreen MacBook Pro
The M6 MacBook Pro and non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models use mini-LED displays. These offer higher contrast and brighter HDR highlights than the Air, plus ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother scrolling and motion.
PROLED XDR: Touchscreen MacBook Pro
The touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models use OLED displays. OLED controls light at the individual pixel level, producing deep blacks without the backlight blooming that can occur with mini-LED. These models also support direct touchscreen input.

 How the screens compare across Apple’s range of MacBooks. 



For most people, the Air’s display is sufficient. Choose a Liquid Retina XDR model if HDR brightness and ProMotion matter to your work. Consider PROLED XDR if you particularly value OLED’s contrast or want touchscreen input.


Is the touchscreen MacBook Pro worth paying extra for?
The touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $400/£400 more than an equivalent non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model. That premium buys display and design improvements, with the same processor options.
What the premium gets you
A tandem OLED display: The PROLED XDR screen offers higher contrast and adds Adobe RGB alongside P3 color support. This may be particularly valuable for photographers, video editors and designers who regularly use the built-in display.
Touchscreen input: Scroll, pinch to zoom and interact directly with content onscreen, alongside the keyboard and trackpad. Its usefulness will depend on your apps and how you prefer to work.
A thinner, lighter design: The 14-inch model weighs approximately half a pound less than its non-touch equivalent. Both sizes also replace the notch with Dynamic Island.
When it’s worth the extra money
The premium is easiest to justify if you spend much of your working day using the laptop’s own screen. The combination of OLED, wider color support and touch could make it a more useful workspace, while the reduced weight benefits anyone who frequently carries their MacBook.
You don’t have to want touch to appreciate the other improvements. As Macworld’s Roman Loyola argues, the display may be the more compelling upgrade.
When to choose a non-touch model
If you mainly work with an external monitor, the upgraded built-in display offers less benefit. A non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max can provide the processing power and memory you need at a lower price.
Touch also won’t suit every workflow. Reaching across the keyboard may be less comfortable than using the trackpad for extended periods, so consider how often you would actually use it.
Compare matching chip, memory and storage configurations before deciding: retailer discounts could make the price difference larger than $400/£400.


						

							


Which is the best MacBook for battery life?
The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro and 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro share Apple’s highest advertised video-streaming rating, at up to 24 hours. For wireless web browsing, the 16-inch M5 Pro leads at up to 17 hours.
The MacBook Air offers a lighter, less expensive option, with both sizes rated for up to 18 hours of video streaming or 15 hours of web browsing. The budget-friendly MacBook Neo has lower advertised endurance, at 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively.
See: MacBook Air, Pro and Neo batteries compared.

How much RAM do you need?
For most buyers in 2026, 16GB of RAM should be the minimum. That is the sweet spot for a MacBook you plan to keep for several years. 
However, the MacBook Neo ships with only 8GB RAM, and there are no options to upgrade this capacity at the time of purchase or later. Whether this is enough RAM depends entirely on your specific use case, as the device is positioned as a budget-friendly entry point into the Mac ecosystem. For the target audience – students, teachers, and casual users – 8GB of RAM should be sufficient for general productivity. A significant concern regarding the 8GB capacity is its long-term viability. 
MacBook memory is not upgradeable after purchase. If you expect to keep your laptop for a long time, it is worth buying more RAM upfront if your budget allows.
RAM recommendations by user type
Casual users and students: 16GB recommended. 8GB is workable for very light use, but not ideal for longevity.
Creative work and gaming: 24GB to 32GB is the safer target.
Professionals and AI-heavy workflows: 48GB to 128GB, depending on workload.

How much storage do you need for a MacBook?
256GB: Fine for cloud-first users with light local storage needs, but it can fill up quickly.
512GB: The better starting point for most people. It gives you more breathing room for apps, files, photos, and offline media.
1TB or more: Best for media professionals, developers with larger local workloads, or anyone who works with large files regularly.
Determining the best storage capacity for a MacBook depends heavily on your specific workflow, as internal storage cannot be upgraded after purchase. 
While Apple previously offered 256GB as a baseline, most current models now start at 512GB or 1TB to accommodate the increasing space requirements of modern operating systems and applications. For most buyers, 512GB is the practical minimum if the budget allows.
Experts now generally advise against 256GB drives for primary machines. Furthermore, SSDs can slow down significantly as they fill up. A common rule of thumb is to buy at least twice the capacity of what you need to store to maintain performance.
Storage (SSD) recommendations by user type
Casual users and students: 512GB recommended. Sufficient for documents, web browsing, and light media use.
General Productivity: 512GB to 1TB recommended. For users with moderate photo libraries and some video projects.
Creative Professionals: 1TB to 2TB+ recommended. Necessary for 4K video editing, large high-resolution photo libraries, and professional audio suites.
High-End Workflows: 4TB to 8TB recommended. For 3D animation, AI development, and massive video production projects.
Is there a difference between SSDs in Apple’s MacBooks
There are significant differences in SSD performance, capacity, and technology across the current MacBook lineup. In March 2026, Apple introduced faster storage technologies for the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models. 
The most notable differences lie in the read/write speeds, which vary based on the model’s processor and the physical capacity of the drive:
MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max): The M5 Pro and Max models, released in March 2026, feature the fastest internal storage in the lineup. Apple claims these SSDs are up to twice as fast as the previous generation. 
MacBook Pro (M6): Apple describes the SSD in the M6 model as “Superfast”. With the arrival of the M5 in 2025 Apple claimed it delivered up to 2x faster read/write performance than its predecessors.
MacBook Air (M5): The M5 MacBook Air also received a similar storage speed boost with the March 2026 update. 
MacBook Neo: The MacBook Neo uses a slower SSD to maintain its lower price point.

Which MacBook chip should you choose?
Choosing the right MacBook chip in 2026 depends on your specific workflow, ranging from basic productivity to high-end professional creative work. Apple’s current lineup features the M5 family (M5, M5 Pro, and M5 Max) and the budget-friendly A18 Pro.
Apple’s MacBook chips currently fall into four clear tiers.
A18 Pro: Best for basic users who want the cheapest MacBook possible.
M5: Best for general users, students, and office work.
M5 Pro: Best for photographers, editors, programmers, and users with heavier workloads.
M5 Max: Best for high-end creative work, large AI models, 3D production, and anyone who needs the most performance possible in a MacBook.

 FAQ 


1.
Which MacBook lasts the longest?
For battery life, the MacBook Pro models lead the lineup, with 24 hours of playback.





2.
Should I buy a refurbished MacBook?
A refurbished MacBook can be a good value, especially if you buy Apple silicon rather than Intel. Just make sure the price gap is meaningful and the machine still has enough life left to justify the purchase.
Since Apple put up prices across the range buying in the Refurbished Store is even more attractive. The MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro were all available at the original price shortly after Apple raised prices. 
For example, the MacBook Neo is $599, you can get a 13-inch, M5 MacBook Air for $1,099 and a 14-inch MacBook Pro, M5 Pro for $2,119.





3.
Is a MacBook Air powerful enough?
Yes. For most people, the MacBook Air is more than powerful enough for everyday work, school, multitasking, web use, and light creative tasks.





4.
Is a MacBook worth it compared to a Windows laptop?
That depends on your priorities, but MacBooks are often worth the extra cost if you value exceptional battery life, premium build quality, class-leading trackpads, and seamless integration with the Apple ecosystem.
Apple’s recent price increases have made Macs more expensive, but the company isn’t alone in raising prices. Lenovo also announced price rises in June 2026, while other PC manufacturers have warned that soaring memory and storage costs are putting pressure on margins, making higher prices increasingly likely across the industry. As a result, the price gap between Macs and comparable Windows laptops may not be as large as it first appears.





5.
How long will a MacBook last?
The typical lifespan of a MacBook is generally between five and eight years, though this depends heavily on a combination of hardware durability and ongoing software support . While the physical components are built to last, Apple eventually classifies older models as “vintage” or “obsolete,” which limits your ability to get official repairs and parts. Find out more here: How long do MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.

title: Apple’s probably done announcing new hardware, but November is still pretty jammed
content:
Macworld





Apple should finally be done announcing new hardware for 2026, but there’s still plenty to be released this month. We’ve got the new MacBook Pro with PROLED, M6 iMac, M6 MacBook Pro, HomeView, and Apple TV 4K that were all announced in October.
There’s some exciting software, too. We expect the OS 27.3 updates to bring more new features, including Audio Intelligence to the Apple Watch series 12 and Ultra 4, as well and the new Health app and perhaps a few other new capabilities. And naturally, we’ll get new Apple TV+ shows and Apple Arcade games, as we do every month. Here’s what we can expect from Apple in November 2026.
New hardware
Apple isn’t expected to announce any new hardware in November, but a lot of the products announced in October don’t actually ship until this month. Here’s what we have on the way.
MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display: The new tandem-OLED MacBook Pro with touch support and the Dynamic Island is shipping on November 6.
M6 iMac: Apple finally updated the iMac with a new processor, though nothing else has changed. It ships on November 6 as well.
iPad mini with OLED: The new iPad mini gets a big upgrade, with an OLED display and an A20 Pro processor. It arrives on November 6, too.
HomeView: Announced last month, the HomeView is the first truly new-category product from Apple in a long time. It doesn’t ship until November 13, so there haven’t even been any reviews yet.
Apple TV 4K (4th gen): The new Apple TV 4K box has a faster processor for Siri AI, built-in microphones, and a remote that has a speaker for Find My. It arrives on November 13.
Apps and software updates
We all get excited about new hardware, but new software updates impact over a billion users and, sometimes, all the cool new stuff is just software that comes to your existing devices. Apple released the OS 27.2 updates at the end of October, which brought several new features.
OS 27.3: Apple’s big OS 27 software updates aren’t done yet—there are still a few significant features to come. Among them are a new redesigned Health app, further enhancements to Siri AI, support for Siri AI on HomePod mini and existing Apple TV 4K boxes.
We expect the OS 27.3 beta to begin in the first week of November, with the final release likely arriving in late November or early December.
Services
Apple TV+
Here are the shows, series, and movies we expect to release on Apple TV+ in November 2026. If you want to know what’s coming later, check our full guide to upcoming Apple TV+ content.
Stick (season 2): A sports comedy about a washed-up ex-pro golfer who coaches a young 17-year-old phenom. November 4
Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook: Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery. November 6
12 12 12: Each episode of 12 12 12 unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist, and the 12 days following. November 13 (Get it?)
Being Heumann: In 1977, young disabled Judy Heumann and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way takes action. November 13
Way of the Warrior Kid: Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc, a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake, a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah. November 25
Apple Arcade
Apple releases most Apple Arcade games in the first week of each month. Check our Apple Arcade FAQ for a full list of Apple Arcade games and more details on the service. Occasionally, games are released with no forewarning, but you’ll usually see next month’s releases listed in the Coming Soon section.

title: Apple Isn't Done With 2026: Here's What's Still Coming
content:
Apple's busiest season isn't over yet. Far from it. With two hardware launch dates still to come in November, plus software updates and new smart home accessories running into December, there's more on the way from Apple before the end of 2026, so be sure to stick around.


Below, we've rounded up what's still coming, along with one date in particular that's worth watching if you're a holiday shopper.


Apple Intelligence testing in China – November 4: The first Apple Intelligence features for users in China enter testing in the latest iOS developer beta from Wednesday, November 4. Apple has partnered with Alibaba to add Qwen support to Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence.

Five new products – November 6: Apple is launching five products this Friday: the OLED iPad mini with A20 Pro (from $699), the M6 iMac (from $1,499), the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 (from $1,999), and all-new 14-inch and 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ models with ‌OLED‌ touchscreens (from $2,899 and $3,399). The latter two are Apple's first touchscreen Macs. Pre-orders are already open, but individual delivery dates vary based on region and configuration.

Apple HomeView – November 13: Apple's new smart home display arrives on Friday, November 13, priced at $299. Available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, the hub can be used to answer questions with ‌Siri‌ AI, display pictures, make FaceTime calls, play music, show recipes, offer up calendar events, and more. Pre-orders are already open in launch markets, but HomeView will not initially be sold in the European Union.

Apple TV 4K – November 13: The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K launches alongside HomeView, and is also priced at $299. Unlike previous generations, there's just the one model with 128GB storage, and it adds ‌Siri‌ AI and supports four-speaker surround sound with HomePod mini 2 or second-generation HomePod speakers. Pre-orders are already open.

Apple Creator Studio updates – November: Updates coming this month bring built-in MotionVFX content to Final Cut Pro, Generate Fill to Pixelmator Pro, and new AI assistants in beta to Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The updates are free for existing subscribers.

Black Friday – November 27: It's not a product launch, but a date likely worth marking. Apple has held a four-day shopping event over the Black Friday weekend in recent years, when it has typically offered gift cards with eligible purchases. Our Black Friday roundup will be tracking the deals.

iOS 27.3 and Apple Intelligence in China – December: Apple has confirmed the public rollout of its first ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features in China for December, alongside iOS 27.3. The initial release is for supported iPhones, with other platforms to follow after the required regulatory approvals.

Apple Home Collection – from December: The new Apple-backed, third-party lineup includes smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple says that availability begins in December, although select accessories will not arrive until early 2027.

Stay tuned to MacRumors for all the latest news, announcements, updates, and deals.

title: Cross-platform Affinity users can finally update as the app comes to the iPad
content:
A year after Canva revamped Affinity for the Mac, it has now released the free iPad version too. Not only is this good for iPad users, but it will free up some Mac ones to update as well.


Designing an education conference program in Affinity for iPad - image credit: William Gallagher
Canva revamped the Affinity suite of publishing and illustration tools on the Mac back in 2025, but it wasn't backwards compatible. If you worked on both the Mac and the iPad, you couldn't update because the two platforms had to stay on the same version.
Now that's over as Canva has released Affinity for iPad. At times it's been referred to as Affinity Studio, but now it is simply Affinity on Mac, iPad, and Windows. It's not just the same name, though, as Canva claims that it has precisely the same features as the Mac version.

title: Apple 'HomeView Ultra' With 9-Inch 360º Screen Detailed in New Report
content:
The Information's Aaron Tilley today reported that Apple has been developing a larger, robotic version of the HomeView. This device has been called a "HomeView Ultra" or "HomeView Max" in rumors, but the final name might be different.


Tilley said a prototype of the device is equipped with a 9-inch display on a swiveling arm, with its overall design said to look similar to Apple's old iMac G4 or Pixar's lamp mascot. Like the HomeView, the device would have standard features like FaceTime, but it would also be "fully aware of its environment and act autonomously."

"The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get off a table," the report said. "It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it."

The report said the device's hardware has largely been finalized for around two years, but there have apparently been "internal disagreements" within Apple, particularly in regards to which software features should be available on the first-generation model or postponed until a second-generation model already being discussed.

The report said Apple is hoping to release the larger HomeView in 2027 for around $1,000 in the U.S., but the device might not be ready to launch until 2028.

Apple has also explored other types of robots, such as one that follows a user around the home on wheels, one that flies inside the home, and one that can fold clothes, but it is unclear if any of these devices will ever be released.

already reported by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who said the 9-inch screen can swivel a full 360 degrees.

title: Best USB-C hubs and adapters for Mac 2026
content:
Macworld





USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.
USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio. USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4. Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

				
					

				
			
Apple




In general, an “adapter” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “hub” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “docking station” or “dock“. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.
Apple sells its own range of USB-C adapters to HDMI, VGA and more, but they are overpriced and underpowered compared to the premium USB-C hubs and adapters we have reviewed here. We haven’t included the many much cheaper but lower-quality versions you can find online as we recommend only from trusted and tested makers. There are plenty of affordable solutions tested and reviewed here that are of a higher quality.
Look for each hub’s video capability for connecting to external displays. Most support only one monitor, but some offer two—note that more than two usually requires an extra software install.
Passthrough power will likely also be of interest to MacBook users. 60W Power Delivery (PD) will work even for the 16-inch MacBook Pro (just), but more watts equals a faster charge.
Note that the ports on the MacBook Neo are USB-C and only one of them is properly data-ready at 10Gbps, with the other just for charging. Read more on how the MacBook Neo’s USB-C ports are different. As it has just one data port, a USB-C hub becomes a must for expanding the Neo’s potential—read our roundup of the best MacBook Neo accessories.
Below the list of our favorite USB hubs and adapters, we describe the types of ports you might require from a hub and what to look for in each.

Plugable has the widest range of USB-C hubs. This $49.95 9-in-1 hub (USBC-9IN1E) is our favorite because it is bristling with top-end ports at an affordable price, and with an unrivaled 125W of laptop passthrough power it’ making’s a great match for larger laptops. A seven-inch cable connects the hub to your MacBook at 10Gbps and a possible 125W passthrough charging when the hub is connected to a powerful enough USB-C charger—that’s the highest passthrough charging we’ve seen in a USB-C hub. 
Total power output from the hub to laptop and devices is 140W. There’s one dedicated 10Gbps USB-C data port, HDMI 2.0 port with 4K 60Hz support, and both SD and MicroSD card readers at fast UHS-II media-transfer speeds. If you need to attach legacy devices there are two USB-A ports, also at 10Gbps. One of these can drive 7.5W of power to the connected device. There’s also a much slower 480Mbps USB 2.0 port that good enough for a memory stick or mouse/keyboard.
Plugable’s $75 10-port USBC-10IN1E is very similar to the 9-port hub but at a more more pro-level with faster 2.5Gb Ethernet and HDM1 2.1 support for a single external display at up to 8K/30Hz, with the option of 4K at an impressive 144Hz refresh rate. Choose this model if you need the more pro-level ports. Unless you need multiple external displays or 40Gbps bandwidth, this hub should offer everything you need for a pro setup in a portable form, but keep reading if you do need a 40Gbps hub.
The $59.99 Plugable 8-in-1 USB-C Hub (USBC-8IN1E) doesn’t just omit one port as you might expect from the name. Like to 10-in-1, it boasts an HDMI 2.1 port so with the right MacBook can display at up to 4K with an impressive 144Hz refresh rate or 8K/30Hz over HDMI 2.1, and this will be the reason you might choose it over the 9-in-1 if your Mac is running at least an M1/M2 Pro/Max or M3 and faster processor. Set against this high-end display support, with the facts that its pass-through power is down to 100W with 85W to the laptop (which should be plenty) and the data connection is also less than the 9-in-1, at 5Gbps vs 10Gbps.
The $39.99 Plugable 6-in-1 USB-C Hub (USBC-6IN1) is similar to the 8-in-1 on data speed and charging, and is also a powerful ally for connecting to high-end displays. It lacks the Ethernet port and card readers, and boasts a third USB-A port if you need that many of the legacy connections. Choosing between the three depends on your display needs and then network and storage requirements.

The $49.99 Anker 555 USB-C 8-in-1 Hub is compact and powerful, offering greater specs than some of the other leading options on this list. It’s one of two similar USB-C hubs from the company, and we start with the best-value option.
The 555 offers two USB-C ports—one that supports 85W USB-C Power Delivery, while another supports data transfers up to 10Gbps. You also get speedy 10Gbps transfer rates through two additional USB-A ports, where many rivals max out at 5Gbps. It’s special as it offers an HDMI port that supports 4K 60Hz resolutions, where most are limited to 4K 30Hz. For 4K 60Hz resolution, your device must support DP 1.4. This includes MacBook Neo, MacBook Air (from 2020), and MacBook Pro (from 2018) and iPad Pro (from 2018). The 10-in-1, 8-in-1, and 6-in-1 Plugable hubs reviewed above go further, supporting 8K/30Hz or 4K/144Hz.
Also included are SD and MicroSD card reader slots. These are rated at UHS-I (104MBps) so not the fastest. If you transfer a lot of data via SD cards, look for a hub with faster UHS-II (312MBps). The Gigabit Ethernet port is great for those times when Wi-Fi just won’t do.
It’s also incredibly light at just under 4.5oz (130g) and compact so you can take it anywhere. At $49.99 / £39.99 it’s hard to deny this hub’s value for money. In our experience, it does get warm with use but Anker says this is normal.

Which extra ports do you need in a hub
Many MacBook users connect their laptop to one or more external displays for greater screen space. You can connect to monitors using USB-C (via adapters to non-USB-C monitors) or better a dedicated video port, such as HDMI or DisplayPort. Check the hub specs to see which displays they support: some are limited to HD displays, others support 4K (also known as UHD) displays. The refresh rate is also important. 4K at 30Hz is fine for most productivity and browsing tasks, but watching video or playing games demands higher refresh rates of at least 60Hz.
You may need some legacy non-reversible USB-A ports, and most adapters and hubs have at least one for your non-USB-C memory sticks and drives. Look for at least USB 3.0, which has a speedy bandwidth of 5Gbps compared to the lamentably sluggish USB 2.0’s 480Mbps.
To fast-charge an iPhone, you need a minimum of 18W and it has to be USB-C, so look for extra USB-C slots with charging power, which are more capable than USB-A.
Other ports to look for in a hub include Ethernet for faster wired Internet access (without the flakiness of Wi-Fi). You can choose from standard Gigabit Ethernet (1000Mbps) or 2.5Gb and even 5Gb and 10Gb Ethernet (2500-10000Mbps), although the faster Ethernet requires the whole network to support that speed.
An SD or microSD card reader is perfect for adding inexpensive portable storage to your system. Card readers come at different speeds: UHS-I at 104MBps, and UHS-II at 312MBps; although some are slower at 60MBps.
Look for hubs that offer passthrough charging, so you can charge your laptop even though you are using up one of the laptop’s USB-C ports for the hub itself. Most don’t ship with a charger, so you’ll need to add your own, and remember that it needs to be a 100W charger to give 85W and above charging if offered by the hub. Lower wattage chargers are fine but will limit the hub’s charging potential. Couple your hub with one of the best Mac USB-C chargers. See how much power your MacBook needs in our advice below the list of recommended hubs and adapters.
You can also buy USB-C adapters for the many older display standards out there, such as VGA and DVI. We’ve picked the best for you below.
Many hubs and docks aren’t compatible with Apple’s SuperDrive CD/DVD drive. We’ve found few dock makers that offers compatibility with the SuperDrive, the Caldigit Thunderbolt Element Hub and OWC Thunderbolt Dock being two that do.
Which ports does each Mac have?
Here are the onboard ports on all of Apple’s current and recent Macs:
MacBook Neo: 2x USB-C (one for 10Gbps data and one for charging), 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Air: 2x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Pro (plain M4/M5/M6): 3x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Pro (M4/M5 Pro/Max): 3x Thunderbolt 5, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
iMac (24-inch): 2x Thunderbolt 4/USB4 or 4x Thunderbolt 4, 3.5mm headphone jack, optional Gigabit Ethernet
Mac mini M4/M6: 3x Thunderbolt 4, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac mini M4 Pro: 3x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack

Mirrored or Extended Modes for Mac displays
When you attach more than one external display to a Mac you can choose between various setups. Most hubs with more than one video port—usually HDMI—can mirror your MacBook’s screen, but most can at best handle showing a different screen to the Mac but not different to each other when attempting Extended Mode.
For full extended Mode, where each of the screens shows a different image and you treat each as an extension to your workspace—moving your cursor and windows easily between the displays—you will likely need a hub or dock that supports free third-party DisplayLink software, which is easy to download and install. Included above are reviews of the Plugable Dual and Quad HDMI adapters, both of which work with DisplayLink. DisplayLink enables multiple screens even with plain M1 and M2 MacBooks that are technically limited to just one external display.

Baseus




How much power does each MacBook require for smooth running
Check the Power Delivery (PD) charging power each hub or adapter offers connected laptops or iPads. 
The MacBook Neo charges at 20W.
The 13-inch MacBook Air charges at 30W, but can fast-charge at 70W and above.
The 13-inch MacBook Pro and 15-inch MacBook Air charge at 70W for fast charging, but even 45W would keep you topped up if running basic tasks at the time. Apple recommends at least 60W for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro.
The higher-end 14-inch (M3/M4/M5/M6, M4/M5 Pro/Max) and 16-inch MacBook Pro require at least 96W for fast charging, but can cope at 60W or 70W. The 16-inch MacBook Pro prefers 140W, but is fine with 94W unless under extreme processing tasks.
You can certainly use a charger at lower power, but remember that it will power up slower than when using a higher-wattage charger, and if too low your laptop might run out of juice altogether when maxed out on power-hungry apps and devices. And you can use a higher-power charger without any concerns. The device being charged decides how much power it requires.

title: Canva Brings Free All-in-One Affinity App to iPad
content:
Canva today released Affinity for iPad, bringing its free all-in-one design app to Apple's tablet, along with a new Sketch Studio built for touch and Apple Pencil.


The release follows last year's desktop app relaunch, which combined the previously separate Affinity Designer, Photo, and Publisher apps into a single app for Mac and Windows. Canva had promised an iPad version in 2026, and says the desktop app has since attracted more than seven million sign-ups.

The iPad app brings sketching, vector graphics, photo editing, and page layout together in one interface. Users can switch between Sketch, Vector, Pixel, and Layout studios while working in the same .af file, which can also be opened on desktop.

Sketch Studio adds freehand drawing with a customizable brush library, while Sketch to Shapes turns hand-drawn forms into editable vector shapes. Photo tools include RAW editing, non-destructive adjustments, and a Mask Tool designed to help trace difficult edges such as hair and fur with Apple Pencil. Elsewhere, layout tools support multi-page documents, master pages, and print-ready output.

Canva says the interface has been designed specifically for iPad rather than scaled down from the desktop app. As for Apple Pencil Pro support, it includes barrel roll, squeeze, and hover, alongside pressure and tilt controls.


The core sketching, vector, photo, and layout tools are free for individuals, but a free Canva account is required to use the app. The only paid-for features are the AI tools, which are locked behind a Canva premium plan – continuing the approach introduced with 2025's desktop relaunch.

The paid features are available through Canva AI Studio and include Generative Expand, image upscaling, noise reduction, and Decompose Layer, which splits a flat image into editable layers.

Affinity's website lists Books, Batch, Data Merge, Quick Adjustments, Info and Scope panels, macro recording, and Astrophotography Studio among the omissions, with more features planned over time.

available on the App Store as a free download with in-app purchases and requires iPadOS 18.0 or later.

title: Apple is now offering iPhone Duo replacements after widespread hinge issues
content:
Macworld





Amid all the excitement and crowds, iPhone Duo launch weekend didn’t go quite as well as Apple hoped. Some fans lucky enough to get their hands on a Duo on day one didn’t have the greatest experience with the new phone, as reports of inner screens cracking began popping up almost immediately. Here’s what’s happening, what Apple has said about the issue, and what you should do if your iPhone Duo starts having screen problems.
Update 11/2: Apple has notified stores of the issue with guidance for technicians on repair or replacement.
What’s the problem?
While many iPhone Duo users have had a flawless experience with their new phone, some users have had similar issues with horizontal and vertical lines appearing on the right-hand side of the inner screen. According to photos on Reddit and across social media, the issue presents itself as a thin vertical line down the middle of the screen accompanied by a thicker line extending horizontally across the right-hand side of the inner screen.
How common is it?
It’s unclear how many units are affected by the screen issue, but there have been widespread reports online from users as well as Apple Store demo units. Most users describe the issue occurring simply by opening their phone. One Reddit poster claimed they only had their phone ”for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.”
As far as we can tell, however, this problem hasn’t been noticed on any of the review units Apple sent out ahead of the launch, so it could be a manufacturing defect that only affected a certain batch of devices.

				
					

				
			Some iPhone Duo owners have experienced issues with the inner display.
Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




What is causing the problem?
It’s not completely clear what exactly is causing the issue, but it appears to be related to the hinge. To investigate the issue during its teardown, iFixit built an exact 3D hinge model and compared it with the reported damage locations. It reports:
The breaks cluster near the transition from the gap for the crossing flex cable to the central hinge support. The damage we’re seeing in photos isn’t right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends. 
All those edges meeting in this spot mean lots of possible culprits. That center pivot looks different from the rest of the hinge. Could it be getting stuck? Could something else be getting stuck?
What we know is that the issues appear to all be causing identical screen problems, so it appears to be related to something under the display. 
Has Apple acknowledged the issue?
In a statement to the media, Apple says it is “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.” It recommends contacting AppleCare (1-800-APLCARE) for a replacement if a user experiences issues with their display. Apple has also issues a memo to Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers of the issue with guidance for technicians to diagnose the issue. 
There are numerous reports of Apple Stores swapping out affected units, but Apple hasn’t issued an official repair program. However, a support page titled “iPhone Duo Troubleshooting Hinge Issues” was published Sunday to offer “steps to help resolve issues,” including:
Device won’t open or close completely
Unexpected noise while opening or closing the device
Loose hinge
Bent or broken hinge
Enclosure damage that affects hinge operation
Apple suggests referring to the iPhone Duo user guide “for device hinge handling and safety guidance,” as well as removing third-party cases or screen protectors, and checking for “particles or dust along the hinge and for dents or scratches on the enclosure.”

				
					

				
			The iPhone Duo’s hinge is causing issues with the inner display on some models.
Britta O’Boyle




What can Duo users do?
While there isn’t an official replacement program yet, Apple says that phones will need to have the inner display assembly replaced. If your iPhone Duo has experienced any of the issues above, you should visit your local Apple Store or call Apple’s customer service number, 800-275-2273, or AppleCare, 1-800-275-2273 (1-800-APL-CARE).

title: Not every Apple product is ‘exciting,’ it turns out
content:
Macworld





Well, in the long list of Apple product launches, last week’s announcements were certainly some of them. Marketing supremo Greg Joswiak didn’t set the bar especially high when he predicted “an exciting week,” but even that comparatively tepid assessment turned out to be wildly optimistic.
The 8th-gen iPad mini falls, I would say, into the category of dull but worthwhile iterative refreshes. It gets some nice upgrades, including a thinner and lighter body, a faster processor, and an OLED screen, but doesn’t alter the fundamental truth that big-screen smartphones, and especially foldables, have rendered mid-price mini tablets largely obsolete… and thanks to another $100 price hike, the mini is now verging on premium. It needed a change of direction, not a costly glow-up.
Tuesday’s twin launches, presumably paired because neither was remotely enough to carry even a website update by itself, saw the arrival of M6 updates to the iMac and MacBook Pro. Apple found itself painfully short of “exciting” things to say about the new iMac; of the six things trumpeted in the summary paragraph at the top of the press release, four also apply to the previous M4 model. The same is basically true of the M6 MacBook Pro. The best we can say about them is that at least the prices are the same. 
It wasn’t until Wednesday that we got a launch that was genuinely groundbreaking (within the Apple ecosystem, at any rate), even if the touchscreen MacBook still strikes me as an offence against logic and reason.
It was a similar story earlier in October. There was one innovative if strategically questionable product, the HomeView, along with a worthy but straightforward new HomePod mini and an Apple TV refresh that costs way too much and has few exclusive features. The Apple Home Collection didn’t exactly set pulses racing either.
Traditionally, when there’s a big backlog of unreleased products, Apple follows its September event with another in October. We expected Apple to group together the Mac and iPad launches as it has so often in the past, build to the touchscreen MacBook as the flagship launch, and then very likely unveil HomeView as One More Thing. But for whatever reason it decided to go down a different route, splitting its remaining fall launches into a pair of low-key “experiences,” followed by a series of quiet press releases and site updates at the rate of one or two products per day. This seems to have become the company’s favored approach for anything less than its most high-profile launches, and there are advantages to making announcements in this way.
Most obviously, it saves on time and money because the marketing team doesn’t have to script and edit a 90-minute show, and busy senior execs don’t need to rehearse and perform a full-length presentation. But there’s the handy side effect that more obscure products get to enjoy their day in the sun. The new iPad mini would have been a minor footnote in the touchscreen MacBook show, for example, but instead it gets to bask in the glow of media and customer attention and be appreciated for the substantial (if in my opinion misguided) refresh that it is. If everything is rolled into an event, it’s inevitable that the smaller items will be lost in the hustle and bustle.
But that same hustle and bustle can sometimes do you a favor. The Apple TV’s missteps were cruelly exposed in the media spotlight, for example, and it might have been kinder to bury those perfunctory M6 micro-updates on a day when something more interesting was happening. 
Then there was the 2nd-gen HomePod mini, which essentially amounted to better AI (in a future software update) and worse colors. This was a necessary refresh, because the HomePod desperately needed Siri AI, and would likely have appeared in a few “important announcements you missed” articles if it was bottom of the bill at a big Apple event. But the HomePod mini was second on the bill at a very small event–sorry, experience–which drew attention to the fact Apple didn’t redesign the speaker or make any substantive non-AI-related upgrades six years after the first one came out. All that focus set a standard of noteworthiness it was never going to justify.
Not every Apple product is exciting, it turns out. But of course we knew that already. The company has found over the past decade or so that small iterative updates generally make the most sense from a financial point of view. The funny thing is that this fall has been unusually interesting: we’ve seen not one, not two, but three genuinely innovative Apple product launches in the form of the iPhone Duo, the HomeView, and the (touchscreen) MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Yet the idiosyncratic manner in which the company has made its announcements has drawn attention to everything else.

title: Here's a New Tour of Apple's HomeView Software
content:
Broadcasts app developer Steve Troughton-Smith has shared a Halloween treat for us today: a tour of the software on Apple's upcoming HomeView smart home hub. Apple has already demoed the HomeView to selected tech reporters and content creators, but Troughton-Smith offers a closer look at several features, interfaces, and apps.


Using a virtualized HomeView created by Guilherme Rambo, Troughton-Smith provided a closer look at the home screen, Control Center, clock faces like Flow and Snoopy, and apps like Timers, Alarms, World Clock, and Settings. Note that while the virtualized HomeView shows an Ethernet menu, the device actually supports Wi-Fi only.






HomeView supports up to six users. The device has a built-in camera that can recognize people and display their personal content in apps like Messages, Calendar, Reminders, FaceTime, and Find My. Rambo and Troughton-Smith have yet to bypass this recognition requirement  with the virtualized HomeView, so those apps are all locked.

Troughton-Smith revealed that the HomeView will have a Liquid Glass slider that lets you adjust how clear or tinted the interface elements look, and he also confirmed that the device's keyboard supports QuickPath swipe typing.






music player, video player in both wide and square formats, and AirPlay pairing interface.

title: Top Stories: Apple's Big MacBook Pro, iPad mini and iMac Updates
content:
One busy week after another for Apple has left our heads spinning, with this week seeing several Mac updates as well as a revamped iPad mini.


All of this week's craziness comes right on the heels of last Friday's iPhone Duo launch, not to mention all of the other products now available or still in pre-order status, so read on below for all of the details!

Top Stories

Everything Apple Announced This Week

It's been a busy October for Apple, and the company ended the month with a bang by introducing a number of new products even as some of the previously announced ones from earlier this month have yet to become available.


If you missed the news over the first three days of this week, we've rounded up all our coverage in one spot, so it's easy to take a look back. All of the new products are available for pre-order now, with a launch set for Friday, November 6.

Apple Announces OLED MacBook Pro With Touch Display

The headliner for the week was Wednesday's introduction of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It's a mouthful, but it's the culmination of several years of rumors about a MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen, plus it includes several other upgrades such as lighter weights, a reinforced hinge to stabilize the display while it's being touched, a Dynamic Island instead of a notch, and even the return of an illuminated Apple logo on the lid.


The new machines are being sold alongside the previous MacBook Pro models with mini-LED displays, with the PROLED models carrying $400 price premiums over their counterparts even though they use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip options.

Apple Announces New 14-Inch MacBook Pro With M6 Chip

The low end of the MacBook Pro family also got an update this week, with Apple announcing a speed-bumped M6 version of the 14-inch base model.


The M6 chip in the ‌MacBook Pro‌ features a 12-core CPU with 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores, paired with a 12-core GPU. This is up from the M5 chip with a 10-core CPU with 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores, paired with a 10-core GPU.

Alongside the M6 chip, the new 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ now features support for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity via Apple's N1 wireless chip. It can also now drive dual external 4K displays at up to 165Hz, up from 144Hz.

Apple Announces New iMac With M6 Chip and More

The 24-inch iMac also got a speed bump this week, with Apple's all-in-one desktop moving from the M4 chip to the M6 for faster performance and adding an N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, faster SSD speeds, and more.


The new iMac has the same design as the previous model, and the color options remain the same: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver.

Apple Announces New iPad Mini With 8.5-Inch OLED Display, A20 Pro Chip, and More

This week wasn't all about the Mac lineup, with Apple also taking the wraps off of a redesigned iPad mini featuring a larger 8.5-inch display that uses OLED technology for the first time.


In addition, the new iPad mini features a thinner and lighter design, an A20 Pro chip, a new Acoustic Display audio system that eliminates speaker holes, IP67-rated water and dust resistance, a landscape front camera, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, and more. Altogether, Apple says this amounts to the iPad mini's "biggest update ever."

Mac Studio With M5 Ultra Now Available With 512GB RAM for $22,299

When Apple introduced the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio back in August, it said that a high-end M5 Ultra option with 512GB of memory would become available in late October, and it's finally here for an eye-popping price of $22,299.


This configuration is obviously only intended for hungriest of power users, requiring the highest-end chip with a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. The memory upgrade alone to increase from the standard 96GB to 512GB costs $15,500.

Crackgate? iPhone Duo Owners Report Screens Breaking Along the Hinge

With all of the announcements this week, it's easy to forget that the groundbreaking iPhone Duo just launched last Friday, and while early adopters have been enjoying much of what Apple's first foldable phone has to offer, it hasn't been entirely smooth sailing.


At least a few users have experienced sudden interior screen breakage seemingly caused by something going wrong in the complex hinge of the device. Apple has said that it is aware of the issue affecting "a small number of iPhone Duo units" and that affected users should contact AppleCare to obtain replacement units.

MacRumors Newsletter

Each week, we publish an email newsletter like this highlighting the top Apple stories, making it a great way to get a bite-sized recap of the week hitting all of the major topics we've covered and tying together related stories for a big-picture view.

content:
Apple today released HomeView Software 27.2, which is the software that runs on the upcoming HomeView device set to launch on November 13.


The HomeView was announced earlier in October, but the early software release gives us a look at features like wallpapers and reveals a few tidbits we didn't previously know.

Wallpapers

There are 20 default wallpapers to choose from on HomeView, with a range of colors. Users will also likely be able to set their own photo wallpaper. The HomeView uses faces, but the wallpapers may be shown on the Home Screen.

Apple today announced that the first iOS 27.3 developer beta will be released next week and enable some Apple Intelligence features in China.


In a press release shared on the Apple Newsroom website in China, Apple said the beta will be released on Wednesday, November 4, but that likely means Tuesday, November 3 in the U.S. due to time zone differences. Apple said iOS 27.3 will then be released to the public in December, but it did not provide a specific date.

iOS 27.3 will enable some of the earlier Apple Intelligence features on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer in China, such as Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up, Notification Summaries, Priority Notifications, Visual Intelligence, and Live Translation with AirPods.


Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features announced at WWDC 2026 will not be available in China on iOS 27.3, according to Apple.

Image Playground will also not be available in China.

Apple also said it has partnered with Alibaba to add support for its AI assistant Qwen within Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence.

title: Apple's Flash Storage Suppliers Are Finally 'Getting Their Revenge'
content:
The Wall Street Journal's Rolfe Winkler this week reported that flash storage suppliers once "bullied" by Apple have been "getting their revenge" on the company over the past year due to a severe memory chip shortage, which stems from AI companies building out massive data centers that utilize significant amounts of flash storage and RAM.


As the iPhone took off, Apple became the world's largest buyer of flash storage, and naturally that gave the company a lot of leverage in negotiations.

Tony Blevins.

"After ordering flash at rock-bottom prices, Apple would refuse delivery at times if flash prices were falling," the report said. "That left suppliers holding piles of unsold chips, including ones custom-made for Apple. Kioxia executives joked they felt like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football—with Lucy always pulling it away."

Based in Japan, Kioxia was previously known as the Toshiba Memory Corporation.

Apple is also said to have "bullied flash makers into opening their books so it could monitor sales, making sure no one else got a better deal."

The report shared another example involving flash storage supplier Sandisk. Apple's other suppliers, such as SK Hynix and Samsung, were not mentioned.

"Around the end of 2015, Sandisk refused Apple's requests to send additional supply because it already had customers willing to pay more," the report said. "Blevins threatened a Sandisk salesman with retaliation, saying he would have Sandisk's chief executive, Sanjay Mehrotra, 'crawl on his knees' back to Apple, according to a person familiar with the call."

Things changed when the AI era arrived.

"Two years ago, Apple bought nearly twice the flash storage of Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Google combined, according to TechInsights estimates," the report said, citing a research firm. "Hyperscalers are now buying double Apple's share."

raised prices on more than a dozen products this year, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, HomePods, the Apple TV, and more, with the company attributing these increases to the memory chip shortage. Apple's former CEO Tim Cook said price increases were "unavoidable."

Apple is not completely immune, though. Higher prices could result in lower demand, and the report said its profit margins on storage upgrades have been impacted. For example, TechInsights estimated that Apple makes a gross profit of $134 when a customer spends $200 to upgrade an iPhone 18 Pro from 256GB to 512GB of storage, down from $185 when a customer opted for the equivalent upgrade for the iPhone 17 Pro last year.

The Wall Street Journal. "We look forward to continuing our important work together."
